content.value: A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Containers isolate applications from each other and from the host system.
Think of it like shipping containers in real life — a standardized box that can hold anything and be transported anywhere. Software containers work the same way: "Build once, run anywhere."

content.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines
content.value:
Virtual Machine:                    Container:
┌──────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────┐
│   App A  │ App B │              │   App A  │ App B │
├──────────┼───────┤              ├──────────┼───────┤
│  Libs A  │ Libs B│              │  Libs A  │ Libs B│
├──────────┼───────┤              ├──────────┴───────┤
│ Guest OS │Guest OS│              │  Container Engine │
├──────────┴───────┤              │    (Docker)       │
│   Hypervisor     │              ├──────────────────┤
├──────────────────┤              │    Host OS        │
│    Host OS       │              ├──────────────────┤
├──────────────────┤              │    Hardware       │
│    Hardware      │              └──────────────────┘
└──────────────────┘

VMs: Each app gets a full OS (GBs, minutes to start)
Containers: Share host kernel (MBs, seconds to start)
Key interview fact: Containers share the host OS kernel while VMs each run their own kernel. This makes containers 10-100x lighter and faster to start than VMs.

quiz.question: What is the main architectural difference between containers and VMs?
options: Containers are more secure than VMs
Containers share the host kernel; VMs run their own kernel
quiz.explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel and only package the application layer. VMs virtualize the hardware and run a complete guest OS, making them heavier.

content.value: Docker uses a client-server architecture with three main components:

content.title: Docker Components
content.value:
Docker Client (CLI)  ──HTTP API──▶  Docker Daemon (dockerd)
                                        │
                                   Manages:
                                   ├── Images (blueprints)
                                   ├── Containers (running instances)
                                   ├── Networks (communication)
                                   └── Volumes (persistent storage)

**Image** — A read-only template containing your application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration. Think of it as a class in OOP.

**Container** — A running instance of an image. Think of it as an object created from the class. You can have many containers from one image.

**Registry** — A storage service for Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.

content.title: Essential Docker Commands
content.value:
docker pull nginx              # Download an image from Docker Hub
docker images                  # List all local images
docker run nginx               # Create and start a container
docker run -d -p 80:80 nginx   # Run detached, map port 80
docker ps                      # List running containers
docker ps -a                   # List ALL containers (including stopped)
docker stop <container_id>     # Stop a running container
docker rm <container_id>       # Remove a stopped container
docker logs <container_id>     # View container logs
docker exec -it <id> /bin/sh   # Open a shell inside a container

quiz.question: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is a running instance of a container
A container is a running instance of an image
quiz.explanation: An image is a static blueprint (like a class). A container is a running instance created from that image (like an object). You can create many containers from one image.

content.value: A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions to build a Docker image. Each instruction creates a layer in the image, and Docker caches these layers for faster rebuilds.

content.title: Example Dockerfile
content.value:
# Start from a base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency files first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm install --production

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Interview tip: Copying package.json before the rest of the code is a Dockerfile best practice. If your code changes but dependencies don't, Docker reuses the cached npm install layer — saving minutes on each build.

content.title: Build and Run
content.value:
docker build -t myapp:v1 .              # Build image, tag as myapp:v1
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:v1     # Run the container

quiz.question: Why should you COPY package.json before COPY . . in a Dockerfile?
options: It doesn't matter — the order is irrelevant
To leverage Docker's layer caching — dependencies are reinstalled only when package.json changes
Because package.json must be read first
quiz.explanation: Docker caches each layer. If package.json hasn't changed, the npm install layer is reused from cache. If you copy everything first, any code change invalidates the cache and forces a full reinstall.

content.value: By default, containers are isolated from each other. Docker provides networking to let containers communicate, and volumes to persist data beyond the container lifecycle.

content.title: Docker Networking
content.value:
docker network ls                          # List networks
docker network create mynet                # Create a custom network
docker run -d --name db --network mynet postgres    # Run on custom network
docker run -d --name app --network mynet myapp      # Same network = can communicate

# 'app' can now reach 'db' by container name:
# postgres://db:5432/mydb
On a custom Docker network, containers can reach each other using container names as hostnames. This is how microservices communicate in Docker Compose.

content.title: Docker Volumes
content.value:
docker volume create mydata                          # Create a named volume
docker run -v mydata:/data postgres                  # Mount volume at /data
docker run -v $(pwd)/config:/app/config myapp        # Bind mount: host dir → container

# Volumes persist data even after the container is deleted

quiz.question: How can two Docker containers on the same custom network communicate?
options: They cannot — containers are always isolated
By using the host's IP address
By using container names as hostnames
quiz.explanation: On a user-defined Docker network, containers can resolve each other by name. 'docker run --name db --network mynet postgres' can be reached at hostname 'db' by other containers on 'mynet'.
